newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen opening mixed.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen opening mixed.

text.p: Wall Street stocks, under pressure from a soft bond market, are expected to open mixed on Tuesday after yesterday's sell-off.
Analysts said the Dow had retraced about half of the losses of its recent correction and it would be difficult to make headway unless bonds perked up.

"There was no volume or breadth to suggest that the move higher was powerful," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "Now that the move is over, it's back to the drawing board in terms of market direction."
"The market is settling down again. That's part of its consolidation," Wachtel said.

Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said that the key to today's action was what happened in Nasdaq after it fell 18.62 points, or 1.52 percent, to close at 1,203.95 on Monday.

"The bashing of the high technologies and the fact that second and third level securities continue to slip is worrisome," Cardillo said. "What we are seeing is an erosion of confidence in lower to mid-cap stocks."
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average closed 7.21 points, or 0.04 percent, lower at 18,544.45 after early gains brought on by a rebound in financial sector shares were eroded in the afternoon session.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 12.8 at 4341.5.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, oil stocks were mostly higher following better-than-expected earnings reports on Monday from Exxon Corp and Amoco Corp.
Texaco Inc , which is expected to book a $488 million tax refund in its first quarter results, due later on Tuesday, was up 5/8 to 105.
Mobil Corp and Chevron Corp were up 3/8 to 125-7/8 and 1/4 to 65 respectively.
The dollar was firmer and hanging on to most of its gains in Tokyo and steady at midday in Europe, holding its gains against the mark.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly lower, with the long bond down 5/32 to yield 7.10.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that investors were ready to run for the exits when market veteran Sir John Templeton, retired chairman of Franklin Templeton Group, uttered the words bear market.

The New York Times Market Place writes that oil profits held up for for the first three months of this year, but oil analysts say that the industry will have a tougher time keeping up such a high level of profitability.
Crude oil prices, which dropped in the first quarter to about $20 per barrel, are expected to fall further to the $18 to $19 range.
